claims.text: The initial alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution with Mg uniformly dissolved in the matrix.
Controlled isothermal annealing triggers thermally activated partitioning from the metastable solid solution.
Partitioning promotes nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Finely dispersed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates can retain corrosion resistance.
Finely dispersed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates can retain high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Intermetallic coarsening undermines corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The size, distribution, and connectivity of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates control the integrity of protective oxide and corrosion films.
Precipitation from the supersaturated metastable matrix is nucleation-controlled.
At lower temperatures, a fine dispersed intermetallic network supports stable passivation.
At higher temperatures, accelerated coarsening produces a connected intermetallic phase.
A connected intermetallic phase compromises protective films.
Annealing within an optimal temperature/time window will produce a controlled, fine bimodal microstructure relative to the initial homogeneous state.
The fine bimodal microstructure will correlate with maintained corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Annealing above the proposed threshold will produce coarse intermetallic phases.
Annealing above the proposed threshold will measurably degrade protective properties.
A service-regime boundary near 450 °C separates fine-precipitate retention from coarse-intermetallic degradation.
The exact beneficial and detrimental temperature/time thresholds may vary with alloy composition.
